md"""
> Our measurement and observation tools are becoming increasingly inadequate in the context of our changing economy.
>
> -- Zvi Griliches, "Productivity, R&D, and the Data Constraint," *American Economic Review*, 1994
"""
156 ms

Griliches' Data Woes

Like many economists doing research in the 1990s, Griliches was concerned that growth in capital and labor explained little of the observed growth in output. Despite forty years of research, most growth was still attributed to a residual called \emph{technical change}–-but this residual could not be easily sourced. Particularly troublesome for Griliches was the productivity slowdown during the 1970s and 1980s across the globe that some pessimists viewed as permanent. Despite the ominous predictions, Griliches was of the view that the glass was not half empty but rather half full. Better measurement would bring a better understanding of the evidence.1

In this chapter, we review the data up to 1990 that Griliches was observing–-although I will purposefully draw from datasets available today so that students can replicate the figures and tables that I create. In the spirit of Griliches, if there is better measurement, why not use it. Moreover, I will show how the world has changed since 1990 given Griliches' prediction that with better comes a better understanding.

We will start with labor productivity measures for different industries to show that sectors viewed as "measurable" by Griliches are becoming an even smaller share of the U.S. economy since the writing of his Presidential lecture. We then explore measures of R\&D and innovation to see if they predict subsequent productivity growth–-again to see if there is any post-1990 evidence that differs from that presented in the 1994 paper.

Share of "Measurable" Sectors

Let's start with one of Griliches' data woes: the decline in sectors that are primarily goods-producing. Griliches viewed goods-producing sectors as "reasonably measurable" because it was possible to construct price deflators–-and thus measures of real output–-from the data collected by the national accountants for estimating GDP by industry. The industries deemed "measurable" were: agriculture, mining, utilities, manufacturing, transportation, and communications. Griliches' "unmeasurable" sectors, which were primarily service-producing included construction, trade, finance, other services, and government.

In Figure 1, we plot real value added per hour over the period 1947 to 1990 in thousands of 1982 dollars–-the same units as in Griliches (1994, Figure 1)–-using data from the BEA-BLS integrated industry-level production accounts. (See Eldridge et al.~(2020).) Real value added is constructed by subtracting real intermediate inputs from real gross output. Sectors are grouped to match Griliches' measurable and unmeasurable distinction as closely as possible. The only tricky decision is the classification of the relatively recent \emph{information} sector, which includes publishing and software; motion picture and sound recording; broadcasting and telecommunications; and data, internet, and other information services. Prior to the switch from the the SIC to the NAICS industrial classification systems, printing and publishing included in manufacturing, communications was included in transportation and utilities, and there really very little in the way of data processing or internet at all.

Figure 1 shows that the total economy in 1950 had an average real value added per hour of roughly $10 (measured in 1982 dollars)–-close to what Griliches reports using earlier data sources. By 1990, the value had more than doubled and had reached $23 (again in 1982 dollars). If we look at the measurable and unmeasurable sectors, we see the same pattern that Griliches saw: a much flatter profile for the unmeasurable sector than the measurable sector. The unmeasurable sector has Real value added per hour in the unmeasured sector is roughly $12 in 1950 and rises to $21 by 1990–-not even doubling–-while the measured sector starts at $7 and rises to $28–-up by a factor of 4.

In Figure 2, we continue the plot, splicing the historical data (up to

  1. with the current 1997–2024 production account file.

The figure clearly shows that the data have gotten much worse. The differences between the measurable and unmeasurable productivities are dramatic. By 2024, real value added per hour is $32 for the unmeasurable sector and a much higher $108 for the measurable sector. Interestingly, the picture does show significant growth occurred during the 1990s–-growth that Griliches suspected would materialize with the computer revolution. However, as the figure makes clear, most of the economy by the end is in the unmeasurable sector and therefore the final estimate for productivity is only $46, well below $108.

We can use the BEA-BLS industry accounts to get more specific about how the distribution of economic activity has changed over time. In Tables 1 and 2, we show the distribution of value-added and hours for two years chosen by the users. The earliest possible year is 1963 given the lack of data availability for major subindustries of the information sector any earlier. Let's start with this as the first year and we will compare this to 2024, which is the latest available. The distribution of value added in Table 1 shows a decline in all industries Griliches called measurable (that is, agriculture, mining, utilities, manufacturing, and transportation (excluding communications under the NAICS classification). By far the largest change is in manufacturing, which fell from one-quarter of the total value-added down to less than 10 percent. Overall, the measurable sector fell from 36.6 percent of value added to 16.3 percent. If users change the last year to 1990, they will find that this was roughly the midpoint of the transition period in terms of both time and the decline in value added. Sectors increasing over time are information; finance, insurance, and real estate; a broad category of services; and government. In the case of hours worked shown in Table 2, the changes are even larger and more concentrated in the broad category of services, which more than doubled over the period.

Perhaps more interesting are the changes in investments in intellectual property products (IPP) over time. This relatively new BEA investment category includes R\&D, software, and artistic originals. In Table 3, I use the BEA Fixed Asset tables by industry and again allow users to compare data in two different years. If we compare 1963 and 2024, we find that the measurable sectors have changed little: they have always invested about one-quarter of all IPP investment. That is because the main investor in 1963 was the government that funded R\&D in defense, energy, space, and so on. Fast forward to 2024 and we see that the private sector now does must of the investment. As in the case of value-added and hours, there is a compositional shift, but since the government is part of the unmeasured sector, the overall statistics do not show a shift to the unmeasurable.

The Role of R&D

A central theme for Griliches was the analysis of R&D spending and its impact on total factor productivity (TFP) growth–-that is, growth in real industry output not accounted for by growth in measured capital, labor, materials, energy, and purchased services. In his Presidential lecture, he noted that estimates of the impacts were modest at best and sensitive to choices of price deflators.

In Figure 3, I show a figure related to that shown in Griliches (1994, Figure 3), with a measure of TFP growth on the y-axis and a measure of R\&D intensity on the x-axis. Here, TFP growth is annualized log growth in the BEA-BLS integrated total factor productivity index from 2012 to 2024. R&D intensity is 2018 BEA-BLS R&D capital compensation, a capital-services compensation flow for R&D assets, divided by 2018 gross output. I include both non-manufacturing and manufacturing since the latter is only a small part of the economy in 2018, but the pattern–-or lack of a clear pattern–-is not that different from the plot in Griliches (1994). If we consider the very high R\&D industries with R\&D capital compensation to gross output over 10 percent, we find two non-manufacturing industries: the Federal government with intensity 13.7 percent and TFP growth of 0 percent and the publishing industries except internet with a 17 percent intensity and TFP growth of 3.5 percent. We find two manufacturing industries with intensities 20.3: chemical products with TFP growth 0 percent and computer and electronic products with TFP growth of 2 percent. In Figure 4, I restrict to just manufacturing, but the take-away is the same: there is not much of a relationship.

Patents Per R&D Dollar

Another barometer for returns to R&D spending that Griliches analyzed is patents per real R&D dollar, where the price index is set so that 1972=1 as in Griliches (1994). Figure 5 shows that there were roughly 438 patent applications sent to the USPTO in 1920 per million 1972 dollars spent on R&D. This estimate fell to just over 5 patents for the same spending 100 years later. We can see from the figure that there was growth in patenting during the 1990s technology boom, but the rise in counts is hardly noticeable unless we zoom into this period.

Glass Half-full?

At the end of his AEA Presidential lecture, Griliches returns to asking: whydon′tweknowmoreaboutthesourcesofproductivitygrowthandthecausesforitsrecentdownturn?″Atthetime,henotedthatthetechnologyresidualhadbecomesmaller,notbecauseeconomicscienceprovidedananswertohisquestion,butbecauseoutputgrowthhadslowedandtherewaslessofagapbetweengrowthininputsandgrowthinoutputtoexplain.Atthesametime,therewasanobvioustechnologyboomunderway.Computerswereeverywhereandthecomputerindustrywasbooming.AsSolowfamouslyquipped,You can see the computer age everywhere, except in the productivity statistics'' (New York Times Book Review, 1987).

In the next chapter, I will talk more about what was happening in the early 1990s when I joined the Federal Reserve but before turning to that, let me elaborate on why Solow said what he said. In the early 1990s, almost no one outside of academia and government research labs had heard of the world wide web or the internet. When I joined the Fed in 1992, I asked the staff where I could find the plugs for my ethernet cable. They had no idea what I was talking about. Art Rolnick, Director of Research, had no idea either but thankfully managed to get ethernet cable throughout the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis once he did. Most computing in the early 1990s was still done using mainframes rather than desktop computers. By the end of the decade, that changed. Cell phones went from being used rarely–-in large part because they were expensive and brick-like–-to pocket-sized. Entertainment was VHS and cassette tapes in early 1990s and DVDs or CDs in late 1990s. For younger children, games were played in arcades and then on play stations at their homes. In fact, by the end of the decade, many activities could be done from the home computer: banking, shopping, emailing, reserving, and so on. We were indeed at the start of a technological revolution.
